questions.text:
Consider the following languages over the alphabet [latex]\sum =\{0,1,c\}: [/latex]
[latex]L_{1}=\{0^{n}|1^{n}|n\geq 0\}[/latex]
[latex]L_{2}=\{wcw^{r}|w\in \{0,1\}^{*}\}[/latex]
[latex] L_{3}=\{ww^{r}|w\in \{0,1\}^{*}\}[/latex]
Here [latex]w^{r}[/latex] is the reverse of the string w. Which of these languages are deterministic Contextfree languages?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L_1=\{0^n1^n\}[/latex]: push 0s, pop on 1s [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] DCFL.
- [latex]L_2=\{wcw^r\}[/latex]: c marks the middle, so the PDA knows when to start popping [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] DCFL.
- [latex]L_3=\{ww^r\}[/latex]: the middle must be guessed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL but not DCFL.

Answer: Only L1 and L2

questions.text: Suppose you want to move from 0 to 100 on the number line. In each step, you either move right by a unit distance or you take a shortcut. A shortcut is simply a pre-specified pair of integers i,j with [latex]i \lt j[/latex]. Given a shortcut i, j if you are at position i on the number line, you may directly move to j. Suppose T(k) denotes the smallest number of steps needed to move from k to 100. suppose further that there is at most 1 shortcut involving any number, and in particular from 9 there is a shortcut to 15. Let y and z be such that T(9) = 1 + min(T(y), T(z)). Then the value of the product yz is_______.
questions.solution:
From 9 you can either step right to 10 or take the shortcut to 15.

[latex]T(9)=1+\min(T(10),T(15))[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] y, z = 10, 15

yz = 150

Answer: 150

Consider the decision problem 2CNFSAT defined as follows:
{ [latex]\phi[/latex] | [latex]\phi[/latex] is a satisfiable propositional formula in CNF with at most two literal per clause}
For example, [latex]\phi =(x_{1} \vee x_{2}) \wedge (x_{1} \vee \bar{x_{3}}) \wedge (x_{2} \vee x_{4})[/latex] is a Boolean formula and it is in 2CNFSAT.
The decision problem 2CNFSAT is
questions.solution:
Each clause [latex](a\vee b)[/latex] gives implications [latex] eg a ightarrow b[/latex] and [latex] eg b ightarrow a[/latex]. The formula is unsatisfiable iff some x reaches [latex] eg x[/latex] and [latex] eg x[/latex] reaches x in this implication graph.

So 2-SAT is solved in polynomial (linear) time by graph reachability.

Answer: solvable in polynomial time by reduction to directed graph reachability

questions.text: Suppose we have a balanced binary search tree T holding n numbers. We are given two numbers L and H and wish to sum up all the numbers in T that lie between L and H. Suppose there are m such numbers in T. If the tightest upper bound on the time to compute the sum is [latex]O(n^{a}log^{b}n+m^{c}log^{d}n)[/latex], the value of a + 10b + 100c + 1000d is _______.
questions.solution:
Find L in the balanced BST in [latex]O(\log n)[/latex], then walk in-order through the m values up to H in O(m).

Time = [latex]O(\log n+m)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] a = 0, b = 1, c = 1, d = 0

a + 10b + 100c + 1000d = 0 + 10 + 100 + 0 = 110

Answer: 110

questions.text:
Consider a hash table with 100 slots. Collisions are resolved using chaining. Assuming
simple uniform hashing, what is the probability that the first 3 slots are unfilled after the first 3 insertions?
questions.solution:
With chaining, each key independently goes to any of the 100 slots. The chance it avoids the first 3 slots is 97/100.

For 3 insertions: [latex]\frac{97\times97\times97}{100^3}[/latex]

Answer: (97 [latex]\times[/latex] 97 [latex]\times[/latex] 97) / [latex]100^3[/latex]
